Although the school board made its selection sometime prior to February 13, no details about the individual or terms of employment have been revealed. And once the announcement is made at the meeting, board members will have a chance to comment,” said Board President Veronica Anderson-Thigpen. People in attendance and on Zoom will have the option to speak during public comment after the announcement. articles.text: Editor: I read with interest articles in the Piedmont Post on February 15th and 22nd about electrification. There are some roadblocks regarding electrification in Piedmont. First off, my wife and I are in favor of electrification. When we moved here from the Oakland Hills a little over a year ago, we put in solar panels and a battery backup as quickly as the Piedmont permit process would allow. We added a 240-volt outlet to charge our Leaf EV. We also replaced the 25-yearold gas cooktop with a new induction one and replaced the old energy hog refrigerator with a new efficient one. We plan some other improvements but found out that we have to upgrade our electrical service from 100 amp to 200 amp to be able to add any additional electrical load. This is where the problems come in and may impact the city’s goals for reducing their carbon footprint. We are in a neighborhood that was undergrounded, and when the city did that, they put in conduits that can only accommodate a 100 amp power cable. We contacted PG&E to find out what we needed to do, and because our power comes from under the street and not an overhead cable, we have to dig a trench to fit the larger conduit and cable. We also have to add a new electrical panel for the power to come into the house, even though we put in a new one when we added the solar panels. Our electrical contractor showed us where the new panel should go, and we contacted PG&E to contract with them to trench and put in the new cable. This is going to cost $400 per linear foot, which could cost us over $20,000. However, when PG&E came to look at the site, they said they could not trench as planned because it would go under two retaining walls, and the panel would need to go in a different location. The contractor said the city of Piedmont Design Review might not approve that because the panel might be visible from the street. We are now waiting for another site visit to determine where the trench can go. At this point, with the cost of the trenching to run the power cable, the fee for the electrical contractor to connect everything, the cost of the panel and other equipment the job will need, as well as the city permit, we’re looking at over $30,000. And we still don’t know if the city will approve the location of the electrical panel. The people we’ve dealt with in the building and design review departments, as well as our contact at PG&E, have all been very responsive and easy to work with; however, we still don’t know how long it will take to get this resolved. We also want to put in a heat pump and remove our gas furnace and water heater, to reduce our (and the city’s) carbon footprint, but we can’t do anything until all this is resolved, and the location of the electrical panel is approved by the city. I don’t know how many other residents will be willing to go through this to help reduce the carbon the city emits. articles.text: Comments made on the subject of pickleball by resident Rick Schiller at a recent Recreation Commission meeting were misinterpreted by the Piedmont Post. We apologize for the error and for the insufficiency of a correction printed in the Post on March 1. The full text of comments by Mr. Schiller on February 21 are: Good evening, I know how thorough this commission is and I read all the correspondence that you had received while we were all waiting, and there’s two themes that seem to come up I just wanted to flesh out from those that perhaps oppose this program. One has been that the Recreation Department has not acted properly, there’s been a bad process and there’s been a biased process. The other is that all venues have not been looked at. Now, fortunately, by the report that I’ve heard tonight from Ms. Putzer, Chelle, it was objective thorough and data driven, and even went far beyond I had imagined. And I think that answers all those questions, I will no longer have to write letters in Exedra, or PCA, or Post, and have people come back at me. And I’m quite serious about that. I mean, there’s been some really irrational comments, I get it that people are afraid of change. Sometimes it’s very difficult. But I’ve lived in the neighborhood a very long time, since 1980, on Fairview Avenue. And I remember when there were hard, hard surface basketball, there’s been a lot of different changes there. This is a big change for people. I understand that. But pickleball has grown phenomenally. It is a phenomenal success that most represents Piedmont in the most favorable possible light. Diane Santos and Art came in today from other cities, just about everybody that comes in says, we’re the friendliest program in town. And when they read the bad press in the Chronicle, every other week about Piedmont, that we’re doing some horrible thing, that our Piedmont police are bad or housing’s bad, all of a sudden, here’s pickleball. And they even say that, like when people come because I’ve volunteered quite a bit to work with staff to do scheduling. When there’s a problem people go, “I’m not gonna go talk to Rick.” So they send people to me, and those people have to deal with me and they still say, this is the friendliest program. This is the friendliest program. And it truly is. Finally, I mean, being involved in pickleball has changed my life. And I hope you put the trial through. articles.text: The Piedmont City Council approved on March 6 a total design budget of $510,285, including a $471,471 agreement with Roseville-based Bennett Engineering Services and a $38,813 contingency, for Phase 6 of the city’s Sanitary Sewer Rehabilitation Project. This phase includes rehabilitation of about 14,200 feet of the city’s sewer system. The project is in accordance with an Environmental Protection Agency consent decree that Piedmont and several other Alameda County cities reduce sanitary sewer overflows and reduce the infiltration of groundwater into their sewer system. To comply with this decree Piedmont must replace a rolling average of linear feet of sewer per year; currently the requirement is around 3,300 feet. Piedmont has approximately 48 miles of sewer pipeline, and about 75% has been upgraded. The completion of Phase 6, which the city put out to bid on August 26, 2022, will leave the city with about 49,000 linear feet left to upgrade, confirmed Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. All past phases of the sewer system rehabilitation have been financed through the State Revolving Loan Fund (SRF) program offered by State Water Quality. The city anticipates that, once approvals are received from the State for the SRF loan, costs for Phase 6 preliminary work – including preliminary engineering, environmental document preparation and grant application preparation – will be repaid. Because the sewer project is a matter of both public and private work, Gonzales said that coordination strategies with private property owners who need to upgrade their sewer lateral – the underground part of the pipe that connects a building’s plumbing from the foundation to the public sewer main – will be ongoing. “We have quarterly meetings with EBMUD, about where their future projects will be and where we should adjust our own resurfacing of roadways. We do the same thing with our sewer; we want to make sure that our utility projects are not going to be occurring on a street that we paved last summer,” Gonzales added. Sewer repair methods are less invasive than excavating and removing old pipe. Pipe lining can be installed remotely in existing pipes without having to excavate. Those with questions about the Sanitary Sewer Rehabilitation Project can contact Daniel Gonzales by email at dgonzales@ piedmont.ca.gov, or by phone at 420-3061.

articles.text: During its meeting on Wednesday, March 1, the Park Commission received an update by Parks and Project Manager Nancy Kent and Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales on city park projects including Piedmont Park, new water stations, and the Linda Park off-leash dog area. Piedmont Park Speaking on the steps under construction in Piedmont Park, by Highland Avenue and Guilford Road, Kent said that “the ultimate plan is to have a small entry plaza at the sidewalk level…[with] three memorial benches and at least two memorial trees.” Despite muddiness on the site through the ongoing rains and a three-week delay due to weather, Kent said that Bay Construction “is still making really good progress.” Gonzales confirmed that the project may be pushed back one month. Plans are underway to add metal fencing around the native plant garden in Piedmont Park. Water stations Kent said that the city has purchased three water bottle filling stations courtesy of a $20,000 donation from the Piedmont Beautification Foundation and a $5,000 grant from CalRecycle. The city hopes to have the fountains installed by July 4. One water station will be installed near the pathway that goes to Community Hall in Piedmont Park, and another installed in the quarry area in Dracena Park. A third will be installed at Coaches Field to replace an existing fountain. Linda Park dog area The off-leash dog area at Linda Park was reopened on February 20, but was closed again on February 24 due to additional rain. Gonzales said “Our hope is to keep this park open for as much as we can, but the reality seems to be pushing us in the other direction … I believe we have rain forecast until mid-month, which means that we are not going to be reopening it … probably for most of this month.” A corner of the Linda Park off-leash dog area after the February rains “Don’t worry. None of their hearing aids work.”

articles.text: The Piedmont City Council approved a final design this week for bulb-outs at the Jerome and El Cerrito intersections of Oakland Avenue on March 6, and authorized city staff to put the project out for bid. pages.text: Wednesday, March 8, 2023 3 City Council approves $510,000 sewer project By Selen Ozturk The Piedmont City Council approved on March 6 a total design budget of $510,285, including a $471,471 agreement with Roseville-based Bennett Engineering Services and a $38,813 contingency, for Phase 6 of the city’s Sanitary Sewer Rehabilitation Project. This phase includes rehabilitation of about 14,200 feet of the city’s sewer system. The project is in accordance with an Environmental Protection Agency consent decree that Piedmont and several other Alameda County cities reduce sanitary sewer overflows and reduce the infiltration of groundwater into their sewer system. To comply with this decree Piedmont must replace a rolling average of linear feet of sewer per year; currently the requirement is around 3,300 feet. Piedmont has approximately 48 miles of sewer pipeline, and about 75% has been upgraded. The completion of Phase 6, which the city put out to bid on August 26, 2022, will leave the city with about 49,000 linear feet left to upgrade, confirmed Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. All past phases of the sewer system rehabilitation have been financed through the State Revolving Loan Fund (SRF) program offered by State Water Quality. The city anticipates that, once approvals are received from the State for the SRF loan, costs for Phase 6 preliminary work – including preliminary engineering, environmental document preparation and grant application preparation – will be repaid. Because the sewer project is a matter of both public and private work, Gonzales said that coordination strategies with private property owners who need to upgrade their sewer lateral – the underground part of the pipe that connects a building’s plumbing from the foundation to the public sewer main – will be ongoing. “We have quarterly meetings with EBMUD, about where their future projects will be and where we should adjust our own resurfacing of roadways. We do the same thing with our sewer; we want to make sure that our utility projects are not going to be occurring on a street that we paved last summer,” Gonzales added. Sewer repair methods are less invasive than excavating and removing old pipe. Pipe lining can be installed remotely in existing pipes without having to excavate. articles.text: Back in uniform again, George Tucker a veteran member of the Piedmont Police Department since 2013, has shed his detective street clothes and now wears his dress blues but with a new title: Sergeant. On March 1, after learning the ropes by shadowing Sgt. Willie Wright for two weeks, Tucker officially became a Sergeant. Born in Southern California, he grew up in San Ramon. He attended Diablo Valley College in 2002 before transferring to Whitworth University in Spokane, Washington, where he played college basketball. – Sergeant George Tucker Piedmont Police Department “I grew up playing sports. I played high school baseball and basketball and played college basketball. Being in that team environment, and having that camaraderie was pretty important to me,” Tucker said. After college Tucker worked for a company selling police, fire and postal uniforms, which gave him his first look into a police station while delivering uniforms and gear. “It’s funny. A lot of guys [I delivered uniforms to] said, ‘Why don’t you just step over the counter and be a peace officer?’ I thought they were crazy, but sure enough, two years later that was the career path I chose,” Tucker said with a smile. Tucker took a basic course in 2010, where he learned penal codes and had his first experience firing a gun. “After that course I knew this was a profession I wanted to be in and that I would love to be a peace officer,” he said. Tucker graduated from the Contra Costa Police Academy in 2011 and started his career in George Tucker (left) receives his sergeant’s badge from Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers on February 22. Piedmont as a traffic officer and motorcycle cop, a role he held for five years. His career advanced to become a field training officer, training recruits new to the department. Tucker became a detective and then embarked on the six month process of studying to become a Sergeant. “It was a tough, grueling process. The (Sergeant) test is about policy and current events and required a lot of reading about leadership. I was lucky enough to be selected as the next sergeant, and I’m honored because I’ve worked pretty hard to get to this point,” Tucker said. Tucker joins current Piedmont Sergeants Robert Jaime, Willie Wright, and Nicole Casalnuovo. “Sergeant George Tucker earned his promotion by consistently demonstrating a high-level of competence and investment in the vision of the Piedmont Police Department by contributing to community safety and equity by continually exemplifying the best of policing,” said Chief of Police Jeremy Bowers. “Being a police officer every day, nothing’s really the same. That’s part of the good and bad of being a police officer. Every day and with each call, something can change. That makes it somewhat exciting, but it also can be dangerous,” Tucker explained. Tucker lives in Dublin with wife Jackie and their 10-year-old son Chase. A badge- pinning ceremony will be held in Piedmont City Hall on March 20.

In Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, the Court decided that the right to privacy guaranteed in the 14th Amendment of the U.S. Constitution did not apply to women seeking a pre-viability abortion. Jackson Women’s Health, known as the Pink House, was the only abortion clinic in the state of Mississippi prior to the Dobbs decision. Following Dobbs, the Pink House relocated to New Mexico, where state law still allows women access to abortion care. On August 5, six weeks after leaving Mississippi, The Pink House West began providing abortions and reproductive health services in Las Cruces across the border from El Paso, Texas. On March 1st, Piedmont resident Karen Joffe delivered two quilts featuring designs and messages to Shannon Brewer, the director of as Cruces Women’s Health Organization. Messages were written by 25 contributors from across the US, including Piedmont, and from as far away as Spain. In the clinic waiting room is the Emmy Award that Shannon received for her role in the documentary Jackson (now on HBO Max). Joffe created the quilt project to honor front line abortion clinic caregivers and their clients. The quilt is an homage to the long tradition of American women quilting as an art form to tell their stories and raise their spirits. HEATING AND AIR CONDITIONING COMPANY

articles.text: Piedmont High School senior Julia Banuelos, has been selected as one of 300 recipients of a national Hispanic Heritage Foundation (HHF) Youth Award. The Youth Awards program honors high school seniors of Hispanic heritage who excel in the classroom, community and for excellence in several categories. This year, nearly 30,000 accounts were created to apply for the Youth Awards. From those, three students are selected as gold, silver, or bronze recipientss for each category in 10 different regions across the country. Banuelos was awarded a Gold Medallion in the Healthcare & Science category. Each awardee will receive a grant to fund their college education or to fund a community service effort that tackles a social issue. The Youth Awards program is the main pipeline to the Foundation that helps prepare the larger Piedmont community are innumerable. She has served on Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC) since middle school, serving as its Co-President as a junior and a senior, and leading a number of projects. “In the depths of the COVID pandemic, many of our traditional fundraising events were canceled, but Julia and her co-Vice president, Sofia Prieto-Black, were particularly creative, persistent and hard-working. They came up with a few fundraising ideas that were all very successful and served to keep our members working,” said PSCS Club Advisor Ken Li. “Julia has bridged the entire range of scouting programs and served at many levels,” he added. articles.text: After a three-year absence, the famed Leonard J. Waxdeck Bird Calling Contest will return to Piedmont High School on Thursday, March 30, at 7:00 p.m., at the Alan Harvey Theater. articles.text: On Tuesday, March 7, Piedmont High School Principal Sukanya Goswami sent a letter to families of high school students regarding an assault that happened during a basketball game in the high school gym on Tuesday, February 7. The text of the letter follows: Hello PHS Community: As we prepare for our Spring activities and events, I want to remind parents that safety is important to all of us. As administrators, we are experiencing a lot of excitement as our teams have performed well at NCS and CIF Regional over the past few weeks. But I want to address an issue that happened last month where there was an altercation between adults and students. There was a physical and verbal assault on one of our students at a varsity basketball game by a parent. This is unacceptable and we have a zero policy for this type of behavior. We want to make sure our students and all spectators feel safe at our sporting events and other activities. As such, the following actions have been taken: • A stay-away letter has been issued to the adult involved. This stay-away order means that this individual will not be allowed on campus for 14 days. • As a school system, we are re-evaluating the policies and procedures in place for communicating with students, parents and the greater community following any critical incident on campus. It goes without saying that we expect all members of our community, adults, and students to conduct themselves in a way befitting the values of the Piedmont Unified School District. Please contact my office with any questions. Sincerely, Sukanya Goswami Principal Piedmont High School

articles.text: What does a focus coach do? I get this question a lot when I tell people what I do for a living – and for good reason. Though ADHD (Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder) is well known, focus coaching for ADHD is still a relatively new concept. I am a former student of Piedmont schools (Havens, PMS and PHS) and I recently started an ADHD focus coaching business called MindsGlowing. I decided to leave my career in tech sales and become a focus coach when I came to realize the unique set of challenges that people with ADHD face when tackling the world around them. I understand these challenges and have faced them in my own life. Before I was diagnosed, I struggled with procrastination, lack of organization, and other ADHD symptoms, It wasn’t until after college when I was diagnosed with ADHD that I began to find relief through medicine and developing systems for myself. After I was diagnosed, I decided to complete a program in Positive Psychology to better understand how the mind works. I now use my certification in Applied Positive Psychology to help people with ADHD achieve their goals. One of my clients is a pre-medical student at Columbia University who has recently been diagnosed with ADHD. We meet Set a timer for 30 minutes and let yourself watch a show or go on Instagram and really enjoy the time. a few times a week for targeted focus sessions where we work on goal setting, craft her to-do lists, and tackling her more difficult projects. My coaching takes many different forms depending on the client, the. day, and a multitude of factors. I customize each session based on my client’s unique goals and challenges because there is no one size that fits the way to coach people with ADHD. I want to introduce one concept called intentional relaxation which I work on with my clients who struggle with procrastination. The idea behind intentional relaxation is: when you’re watching TV or scrolling through Tik Tok when you’re supposed to be doing something else, it doesn’t feel very good. It becomes hard to enjoy the thing you’re doing when you’re worried about the things that need to get done. To try intentional relaxation you want to set aside time where you are aware that you’re relaxing and can enjoy it more fully. The best time for this would be when you don’t have too much to do. You can also use it as a break between two tough tasks or in between school and doing homework. Set a timer for 30 minutes and let yourself watch the show or go on Instagram and really enjoy the time. Then once it’s over, you’ll have more energy to complete the task at hand. Check back next month for more on ADHD, focus coaching, and positive psychology tips. Erica Monical is the founder and focus coach at MindsGlowing and a monthly columnist in the Piedmont Post. She can be reached at 415-680-6990 or mindsglowing@gmail.com.
articles.title: Focus coaching helps people with ADHD thrive

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. articles.text: Micah Temple An astronomer peers up at the cosmos through the lens of a telescope; a Navy researcher pours over blueprints below deck; and an engineer sketches the future hull of a ground-breaking rocket. Though each of these feats is remarkable, the three female minds who performed them have been largely unsung. However, an anonymous Piedmont donor is working to change that. At a Makers fundraiser, a donor purchased naming rights being offered for the three workspaces in the high school’s new STEAM building. Piedmont Makers plans to host a Grand Opening for the new areas on Saturday, April 29. The first of the three spaces is one of the building’s most defining features; the cage-covered engineering patio. The patio is set to be named after Annie Jump Cannon, one of the first women to contribute to the field Engineer Raye Montague frequently briefed the Joint Chiefs of Staff and taught at the U.S. Naval Academy in Annapolis, MD. Annie Jump Cannon, was not only a pioneer for women in astronomy, she did so after becoming deaf at the age of 30. Mary Golda Ross was depicted on the 2019 Native American $1 coin by the U.S. Mint for her contributions to the U.S. space program. of astronomy. Cannon developed an instrumental classification system for stellar bodies, known as the “Harvard Classification Scheme.” The second space set to be renamed is the Engineering Lab, used for everything from crafting electric guitars to building complex robots. The lab will be named after the first known female Native American engineer, Mary Golda Ross. Ross’ fame derives primarily from being one of the founding engineers for an elite and highly secretive aerospace project, as well as her immense contributions to the Agena Rocket. The last of the three spaces is the PHS computer lab, to be named after Raye Montague, one of the first Black female naval engineers in history. She’s known for her work modeling a digital rendering of a navy ship as well as being the first female program manager in the U.S. Navy. Three plaques created by students of the Piedmont Makers organization will be unveiled at the grand opening, celebrating the three women’s lives and accomplishments. Will Becker and Micah Temple are Piedmont High School students and interns with the Piedmont Post.
articles.title: High School STEAM lab honors women of STEM

articles.text: This year’s Spring Fling will be co-chaired by Piedmont elementary school parents Catie Osborn and Anne Wheeler. Osborn and Wheeler will work with the Piedmont Education Foundation to plan the annual event. “When I learned about the possible reductions in the school budget for next year, I wanted to do something to help,” said Osborn, “I have a background in fundraising and saw Spring Fling as an opportunity to really make a difference.” Spring Fling is scheduled for May 6, but the months leading up to it are packed with events that contribute significantly to elementary school fundraising. Parent sponsorships are a popular way to support the elementary schools, with three sponsorship levels. This year’s sponsors will enjoy a magical evening on April 6 at the elegant King Avenue home of Melissa and Ali Partovi. Guests will be fêted with cocktails and a feast of savories by noted cook- 2023 Spring Fling Co-Chairs Catie Osborn (left) and Anne Wheeler book author and Chez Panisse Chef Anthony Tassinello. Sponsorship information is available at PiedmontSpringFling.org. “My oldest just started at Wildwood last year, so we haven’t yet experienced the Spring Fling tradition. I want to help with the relaunch by creating some unforgettable events that bring us together as Piedmonters,” said Wheeler. Funds raised through Spring Fling sponsorships, auctions and events directly support Beach, Havens, and Wildwood elementary schools. PEF works with the three school principals and parent club presidents to determine the greatest need.

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team’s magic winter season came to a close on Saturday, March 5 at Binks Rawlings Gym, where the No. 1 seeded Highlanders suffered a surprising 48-45 loss to No. 5 Salesian in the CIF Open Division Regional Semifinals. It was a night when the ball just wouldn’t go in, and seemingly every bounce fell the way of Salesian. “It was a very interesting game. We didn’t shoot it well and we turned the ball over much more than usual. The stars were just lined up the wrong way, and we just couldn’t get it going,” said coach Bryan Gardere. It was a strong defensive game for both sides, Piedmont led 10-7 to end the first quarter and went into halftime holding a razor-thin 22-21 lead. Salesian inched ahead with a 34-33 lead heading into the fourth quarter, but the Highlanders couldn’t find their way back to the front. There were 10 lead changes in the first three quarters. Natalia Martinez led Piedmont with 20 points, but fouled out near the end of the game. Eva Levingston had 11 points, Trinity Zamora and Maddie Hill had six, Adrienne Blackwell had two. “You have to give Salesian credit. It wasn’t a high scoring game, and a lot of things didn’t go our way. I don’t want to take anything away from our year, and that’s the hardest part,” said Gardere. Regardless of Saturday’s result, this was an historic season for Piedmont. They captured their first Western Alameda County Conference championship, won their first North Coast Section banner since 2006, and closed the season with a stellar 27-1 overall record. “We won 27 games, so it doesn’t feel very good now,” said Gardere, “Overall, the girls did a great job; it was an amazing year. It was so much fun, and we had great support throughout the community.” Saturday’s game in the Rawlings Gym was a rocking environment, with more than a capacity crowd. The game had to be halted for a short while in the second quarter due to too many people standing along the baseline Staff Photos Natalia Martinez led Piedmont with 20 points but fouled out in the final minutes against Salesian. Trinity Zamora takes the ball up court in her final appearance at Binks Rawlings Gym. searching for a seat. It was a special time for girls’ basketball and a scene rarely seen since the days of the famous Paris twins. “When you think about it, this senior class had the pandemic hit their freshman year later that spring. This team missed out on having those camp appearances with kids and making an impression on them. It was awesome for them to finally get that connection now that fans were back,” said Gardere. “We had an amazing group of young ladies who hopefully inspired the next group of girls,” said Gardere, recalling young kids lining up for autographs of his players. Departing from this year’s team will be a massive group of Zamora, Hill, Levingston, Perseas Gioukaris, and Blackwell. But continuing is Western Alameda County Conference 2023 Player of the Year, Martinez. “She’ll be the main focus for sure next season. Nat is one of those rare players and deserves all the accolades coming her way. She’s going to see a lot of different defenses next season, and I’m sure she’ll rise to the challenge.” Martinez is set to be named Cal Hi Sports’ Scholar Athlete of the Year, and is an in-demand prospects who has yet to announce her collegiate plans prior to finishing high school in one year. In addition to Zamora, Gardere also expects Levingston, Hill, Gioukaris, and Blackwell to announce collegiate basketball plans in the near future. articles.text: Piedmont High’s Cinderella season in sports came to a close on Thursday, March 2 at Marin Academy, when the Highlander boys’ soccer team, seeded no. 4, lost 4-0 to the eventual CIF Division 4 NorCal champions, the No. 1 seed, in the Regional Semifinals. To get there, PHS defeated No. 5 Kimball 2-0 at Witter Field on Tuesday, February 28 with goals by William Daniel and Enzo Bernales. For Marin Academy, it was a bit of a surprise to see them put in Div. 4 after losing the Division 3 final in penalty kicks with No. 2 Terra Linda. The Wildcats have now won three CIF NorCal titles, winning the D2 crown in 2022 and 2019. All four goals on March 2 were scored by League MVP Malcolm Zalayet, a junior. “It was tough to take. We were in it for the first 20 and gave them some problems, but Marin Academy’s class showed, said PHS coach Todd Sullivan. “They were able to move it around and find some gaps, and that’s what a proper team does. It was great exposure for our guys to play a top team and see what I aspire our program to be.” Piedmont’s Regional Semifinals appearance was the furthest Piedmont High has gone in post-season playoffs since the new CIF tournament started in 2018. PHS lost in 2022 to No. 3 Sacred Heart. “It’s hard to put into words just how great this season was,” said captain T.J. O’Neil, a senior.” It was such a great group of players who came together as a team. At Junior striker Aiden Woolwine will lead a potentially potent attack next year. Sophomore Enzo Bernales scored a penalty kick against No. 5 Kimball. He finished his season as Piedmont’s leading scorer. the beginning of the season, we set our long-term goal to get to the NCS Final. We have full confidence in our coaching and our players. Being able to win NCS and take it a few steps farther makes me so proud.” “This season was about building off of what we did last year. To win it in 2022 and then come back to win it again was such an amazing feeling,” added junior striker Aiden Woolwine. The loss closes Piedmont’s season with a 13-6-5 (W-T-L) record and a second consecutive North Coast Section championship after upsetting No. 1 Cardinal Newman, and then No. 5 Healdsburg and No. 2 University on their way to the banner with the No. 8 seed. Looking ahead to next year, Piedmont will have to replace 14 seniors on this year’s roster and will be in their second season in the Foothill (upper) division of the Western Alameda County Conferencel. But returning to the roster will be routine starters like Woolwine, Bernales, and Sam Shelby, while Gianluca Bini, Bosco Lorin, Rylan Nelson, and Riley Stratman all progressively earned larger roles. “I’m excited to play alongside those guys. They are going to be scary, especially with our other seniors coming up. We’ve built a strong connection and it’s just continuing to build and connecting to find that fluidity on the field,” said Woolwine.

The match closes PHS’ year with a 13-1-6 (W-T-L) overall record and its first Division 4 North Coast Section title in 20 years. “It was a really special team. I told the girls this was the best team I’ve ever had. Anything after winning the NCS title is a bonus, I’m so proud of this team,” said PHS coach Dan Chubbock. Seqouia struck first in the 13th minute when Nina Mills jumped on a ball in a passing lane to play a ball over Piedmont’s back line. Emily Fitzgerald (right) scored Piedmont’s only goal against Sequoia. Audrey Lam (left) finishes her distinguished career at Piedmont as the 2023 WACC Player of the Year. Photos by Todd Marshburn Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team ended its season with an overtime loss to No. 1 Sequoia in the first round of the D3 CIF NorCal tournament. On the volley, Mills sent a shot over goalkeeper Morgan Hunt. But with just eight minutes left in the game, Emily Fitzgerald continued her playoff form and scored on a beautiful right-footed rocket over the keeper’s head. In the buildup, Audrey Lam used a slide tackle to push the ball to Hailey Marshburn, the player who scored the game-winner in the NCS Final. Marshburn sent a long ball from deep in Piedmont’s defensive third to freshman Miranda Liu. Liu, using her speed, accelerated in front of the defender and sent a back heel pass to Fitzgerald while in between three defenders. Fitzgerald pounced on the ball, taking a touch with her left foot and followed through with the right, flying through the keeper’s hands and into net for a 1-1 tie. Piedmont couldn’t find any looks at net in regulation time, but drew several corners and free kicks. In overtime, Marshburn had a shot on target to the bottom left corner five minutes into the first overtime period, forcing a diving save. Piedmont looked like the better side in overtime, pressing forward and winning possession in good areas. However, Sequoia scored on a swift counterattack for the game-winner with three minutes left. Fitzgerald departs as one of Piedmont’s most successful NCS postseason players in school history with 10 goals in nine North Coast Section appearances, “She’s always been one of those players who turns up for big games. She loves to compete and play against the best teams,” said Chubbock. Lam was also a two-year starter for Piedmont and joined the program after spending time with the U.S. Women’s Youth National Team. She is one of the most accomplished soccer players in PHS history and her impact as a maestro in the midfield was easy to see—bringing a flair on the field rarely seen at the high school level. “It was a joy to watch Audrey. She’s already such an accomplished player and has played at really high levels, but you can tell how much winning NCS meant to her. She was ecstatic alongside her teammates,” said Chubbock. When looking ahead to next season, Piedmont will have to replace 10 seniors, but will return some key starters including Liu at striker, midfielders Arden Sorensen-Wald and Louisa Symkowick, and defender Elle Ruegg.

articles.text: Piedmont’s track and field team is off and running in its first year under new head coach Pouyan Assadi. They began their season on Saturday, February 18 at the Grizzly Invitational at San Lorenzo HS, then competing in the Sunset Invitational at Kezar Stadium in San Francisco on Friday, March 3. The final event was the Dan Gabor Invitational at Amador Valley HS in Pleasanton the following day, March 4. “The sprinters, jumpers, and throwers seemed to pick up right where they left off from the 2022 season,” said Assadi. Referring to the Sunset Invitational at Kezar, he said, “It was an impressive outing by a young but confident group under the bright lights at the historic San Francisco venue. The Sunset Invitational has over 500 athletes competing from 30 schools.” Saturday’s event at Amador Valley focused more on distance runners. Returners like senior Christian Taylor finished 2nd of 241 runners in the 800 with a time of 1:59.40. He was also 6th out of nearly 400 runners in the 1600 with a strong early-season time of 4:23.44, a personal record. “A very impressive outing by our distance crew on Saturday night at the Dan Gabor Invitational. Christian Taylor led the way with a silver medal in the 800. And new PRs were made by Christian, Parker Long, Xander Schulte-Sasse, and Alex Aubrecht,” said Assadi. Dan Gabor Invitational results Aside from Taylor’s impressive display at the invitational, Xander Schulte-Sasse placed 8th of 241 in the 3200 with a time of 9:40.02 for a personal record of seven seconds. articles.text: Despite low numbers, team looks strong It’s been a strong start to the season for Piedmont’s baseball team, winning their first three games of the season by outscoring their opponents 40-18. They opened the season beating Lick-Wilmerding 14-6 on February 25 in San Francisco, won 12-8 over Justin-Siena on Thursday, March 2 in Napa, and won their home opener 14-4 over Albany the following day on Friday, March 3. Evident by the scoring output through the first three games, the team is going to be carried by its cast of returning players, Michael Aikawa, Ryan McConathy, Markos Lagios, Peter Krumins, Dimitri Papahadjopoulos, and Liam Campbell. “We definitely have some returning talent and some players who are playing varsity baseball for the first time. We have a blend of an influx of talent and players who have been here for four years like Mike [Aikawa],” said coach Eric Olsen. This is all despite having just 11 varsity members on the roster, requiring Olsen to frequently pull from his junior varsity roster. However, the lack of numbers means Olsen will mix-and-match the pitching rotation. Six players have appeared on the mound with junior Seve Sanchez leading the way with seven innings pitched and four strikeouts. Piedmont was bumped up to the Western Alameda County Conference’s Foothill Division after winning last year’s Shoreline title over Encinal. The Highlanders will face larger enrollment schools like Arroyo, Alameda, Berkeley, Bishop O’Dowd, Castro Valley, and San Leandro. “As a coach, having a smaller roster is great because you can give individual attention and really coach each kid. articles.text: One wouldn’t expect a small town of just over 11,000 to produce a growing group of talent in the sport of fencing. During the week of February 17-20, the Piedmont Fencing Team sent four PHS student-athletes to the 2023 Junior Olympics in Denver, Colorado. The group included freshmen Niko Kalamas and Jonah Kim, and sophomores Oliver Greenebaum and Teresa McKay. It’s one of the most prestigious events for junior fencers. Piedmont Fencing Team coach David Sinkkonen has watched the program build from just six members 10 years ago to nearly 70 in multiple skill levels today, The fencer train in the Piedmont Community Church gym. “Fencing is a very difficult sport; it takes a really long time to build a successful program because it takes a long time for students to develop. Last year, we didn’t have anybody that made it [[to Junior Nationals]. What’s great is that fur of them (Kalamas, Kim, Greenebaum, McKay) all qualified for National Championships in July. These kids have been working hard, and this sport takes a lot of patience,” said Sinkkonen. The re-introduction and resurgence of fencing in Piedmont is quite a surprise to some/ Recently Piedmont’s best known fencer Oliver Greenebaum (left), Niko Kalamas, and Teresa McKay of the Piedmont Fencing Team. was Rafaella Gomes, PHS Class of 2021, who trains at the prestigious Massialas Foundation in San Francisco, and is a member of the Brazilian National Team. “It’s pretty unusual. It’s not a mainstream sport, although there are a lot of people who compete at events like the Junior Olympics. Everyone is probably very aware of the track team, basketball, football, and baseball, but there’s this little fencing program that we’ve built from basically nothing,” said Sinkkonen. articles.text: San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SF MOMA) is currently exhibiting the work of Bay Area-based artist Joan Brown, comprising 80 colorful paintings and sculptures from the celebrated artist. The exhibit ends on Sunday, March 12. Brown (1938-1990) is considered one of San Francisco’s most important local artists. She was once dismissed by critics as ‘unserious,’ but was recognized for her influential artistry after her untimely death in 1990. Works on display include The Dancers in a City #2 and Gordon, Joan and Rufus in Front of S.F. Opera House, which both show how much influence the city of San Francisco had on Brown’s art. Her work was included in SFMOMA’s annual exhibits in both 1957 and 1958. She was the youngest artist exhibited as part of Young America 1960 (Thirty American Painters Under Thirty-Six) at the Whitney Museum of American Art. “We are thrilled to present Joan Brown, a reassessment of the unabashedly personal, defiantly independent and enduringly relevant career of one of San Francisco’s most important local heroes,” said Janet Bishop, Curator of Painting and Sculpture at SFMOMA. Visit https://www.sfmoma. org/exhibition/joan-brown/ to learn more. Museum hours are 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Fridays through Tuesdays and 1 to 8 p.m. on Thursdays. The museum is closed Wednesdays. The Joan Brown exhibition at the San Francisco Museum of Art remains on view through this Sunday, March 12.

articles.text: Photo by Stella Olivier Vocalist S’busiso Shozi in William Kentridge’s Sibyl Cal Performances will present the U.S. premiere of South African visual artist William Kentridge’s newest production, Sibyl, from Friday to Sunday, March 17-19. Kentridge is well-known for his animation artwork and films, as well as design of theatrical productions. His latest opera, Sibyl, is told in two parts and is inspired by the Greek myth of the Cumaean Sibyl, a prophetess of Cumae, a Greek colony located near Naples, Italy. In Greek mythology, a “sibyl” refers to a woman, usually of prodigious age, who is reputed to possess powers of prophecy or divination. The first part of the opera, entitled The Moment Has Gone, will feature the U.S premiere of a film by Kentridge, accompanied by live music, with a piano score by composer and music director Kyle Shepherd and an all-male vocal chorus led by choral composer Nhlanhla Mahlangu. The second part of the opera, Waiting for the Sibyl, features nine vocalists and dancers – as well as Kentridge’s famous medium of animation. Music for Sibyl is composed and conceived by Nhlanhla Mahlangu and Kyle Shepherd. A post-performance discussion with the artists and Cal Performances artistic director Jeremy Geffen will take place on Sunday, March 19. articles.text: The annual Making History concert by Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir will take place on April 22. It will feature the world premiere of Robin Estrada’s Nag Iibang Hangin (Changing Winds) and the premiere of Artistic Director Eric Tuan’s In the Desert. Featuring premieres of new works, past commissions, and up and coming exciting new voices in the choral landscape, the concert – an annual celebration of new music – features all four of the choirs’ advanced performing ensembles. The world premiere of Berkeley composer Robin Estrada’s Nag Iibang Hangin was commissioned by the choir. It describes the two seasonal winds in the composer’s native Philippines and juxtaposes western composition with traditional Filipino vocal and musical forms and practices. Continuing the choir’s commitment to uplifting women composers and BIPOC voices, the program also includes works by Stacy Garrop, Meredith Monk, Rhiannon Randle, and Eric Tuan’s Taloowa Chipota (Children’s Songs), a two-movement work evoking traditional stomp dancing by Jerod Impichchaachaaha Tate, the Composer-in-Residence of the Chickasaw Nation. articles.text: Roy Eaton Roy Eaton. You probably recognize his name because he is often featured on our local music station. In an atmosphere often overpopulated by negativity, Roy Eaton is a breath of fresh air… An inspiration. Let’s see why. The first time I heard Roy Eaton on the airways, I was somewhat confused by what I heard. The sound quality of the recording told me that it was a modern recording, but the piano playing harkened back more than 100 years. There was a gentle resonance in the touch which reminded me of the great Polish pianist-statesman Paderewski. The phrasing was noble and the rhythm was slightly wayward, but in a way that made perfect sense. His Chopin was classic and his performances of Scott Joplin Rags sounded as if the composer were playing them. I asked myself: “who is this guy?” What I discovered is the essence of this article. Eaton was born in Harlem way back in 1930, the son of Jamaican immigrants. His talent was recognized early and he was playing concerts and winning prizes almost from the beginning. Running parallel to his achievements were the prejudices he suffered as a black man. How he overcame them is an inspiration. I was very interested to see a video interview. One of the things that Roy Eaton said was that black kids need to have good role models in life and also in classical music. Even at his advanced age he continues to go to schools to motivate kids. How about that for an inspiration! In many ways, Roy Eaton reminds me of my high school music teacher, Samuel Rodney Browne (1908-1991). There is a very good interview of Mr. Browne where he tells about overcoming the same prejudices. The coincidences are startling. We are never too old to have good role models – nor too young. Usually we think of a role model as an adult influencing a young person, but sometimes the influence is the other way around. I think of this every time I hear the concerts of the Kensington symphony. The Kensington symphony has Geoffrey Gallegos as its conductor and Music Director. The results are musically gratifying because he is a real maestro. I recognized his talent when he was in the eighth grade. If you haven’t guessed, Geoffrey was a student of mine. articles.text: Piedmont Chamber Orchestra to perform at PCA Orchestral musicians relish their opportunities to perform in chamber music ensembles, emerging from the crowd to highlight their artistry in small groups, where everyone gets a chance to shine. Such will be the case this Sunday, March 12 at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, when members of the home-grown Piedmont Chamber Orchestra present a program of three nineteenth-century chamber pieces. After last fall’s enthusiastically received orchestra concert, several audience members urged the PCA to organize a chamber music concert to put the orchestra’s fine players in the spotlight. The PCA has shown through the years that it is a superb venue for chamber music. The string sections will be showcased in Tchaikovsky’s Serenade for Strings, Op. 48, whose main themes have been widely popularized in film and song. The woodwinds and horns will be featured in Franz Lachner’s Octet for Winds, Op. 156, by probably the most accomplished 19th century composer few have ever heard of. An added confection will be the Theme and Variations from Beethoven’s Trio for flute, bassoon, and piano. This program is a first-time addition to the orchestra’s usual fall and spring concerts at the PCA. The orchestra’s conductor, Marty Stoddard, will conduct the Tchaikovsky and play flute in the Beethoven.

articles.text: The Sophie Florence Trio is coming to town for a concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Friday, March 17 at 7:30 p.m. Sink back into the mid-20th century, to a night of nostalgia as the Sophie Florence Trio revisits the songs of Ella Fitzgerald, Dina Washington and Patsy Cline. articles.text: A scene from Disney and Pixar Animation Studios’ The Good Dinosaur After reviewing more than a few kids’ movies, animated and live/action, or features with a seamless blending (thanks to CGI technology), I’ve become well acquainted with the extraordinary art and imaginative storytelling that’s involved. And then I find that I must remind myself to keep in mind who the audience is. That would be those young budding film critics, some dedicated cinephiles, who are content to be told a good story, one with solid visuals, while they remain ever forgiving when animals (or giant reptiles) take on distinctly human characteristics (e.g. speech or expressions). Disney-Pixar’s film The Good Dinosaur fits nicely in the above framework. The narrative focuses on a young dinosaur named Arlo (Raymond Ochoa). He falls into a raging river and is knocked out. When he awakens he finds that he is a long way from home and is in distress. He discovers that he is separated from his family, Poppa Henry (Jeffrey Wright) and Momma Ida (Frances McDormand). With the help of a feral, streetwise pre-verbal Neanderthal cave boy (Jack Bright) named Spot – someone who can snarl and howl with the best – the two set out on a harrowing journey with the ultimate wish to be reunited with home and family. Along the way they meet a menagerie of creatures, some friendly, others not so much. Of course, there are also obstacles to overcome. For the young audience to enjoy The Good Dragon it’s not necessary to be able to identify the cohort of dinos that the duo meet in their travels, each having a salad of vowels and consonants as part of their names – think velociraptors and pterodactyls. They also encounter a family of T-Rex ranchers, led by Butch (Sam Elliot plus his cowpoke partners). The story is a simple one and follows a familiar formula that kids will find entertaining. As expected, it has a right ending for both Spot and Arlo, reminding kids that the fun is in the journey as well as the destination. The Good Dinosaur. Directed by Peter Sohn. From Disney and Pixar Animation Studios. Voiced by Jeffrey Wright, Frances McDormand, Marcus Scribner. 1 hr., 32 min. Rated PG. Released 2015. Now streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Disney+.

articles.text: Walter Becker was co-founder of Steely Dan and a co-founder of the rock and roll Hall of Fame. Steely Dan founders Donald Fagen (keyboard, vocal) and Walter Becker (guitar, bass, backing vocal) were both attending Bard College in Annandale-on-Hudson, New York in 1967. Fagen walked by the Red Balloon Café and heard Becker playing guitar. “I hear this guy practicing and it sounded very professional and contemporary, like a black person, really”, Fagen recalled. He asked Becker to form a band together and they began writing songs. They had trouble finding talented musicians at Bard. One of their early bands was “The Bad Rock Band” with comedic actor Chevy Chase on drums. Becker said, “it was like the Kingsmen (of Louie Louie fame) playing Frank Zappa material”. Out of necessity, Becker and Fagen toured with Jay and the Americans. In 1972, they met producer Gary Katz, who hired them as staff songwriters for ABC/Dunhill in Los Angeles, where he had just become a staff producer. Katz suggested that Becker and Fagen form a band as a way to record their songs, and Steely Dan (who took the name from a sex toy in William Burroughs’ Naked Lunch) was formed shortly afterward. Recruiting guitarists Denny Dias and Jeff “Skunk” Baxter, they released their debut album “Can’t Buy a Thrill” in 1972. With Katz, Becker and Fagen gradually changed Steely Dan from a performing band to a studio project, hiring professional musicians to record their compositions. Though the band didn’t perform live between 1974 and 1993, Steely Dan’s popularity continued to grow throughout the ‘70s as their albums became critical favorites and their singles became staples of AOR and pop radio stations. In 1981, Becker and Fagen parted ways. The following year, Fagen released his solo debut, “The Nightfly,” which became a hit. Even after the group disbanded in the early ‘80s, their records retained a cult following, as proven by the great success of their unlikely return to the stage in the early ‘90s. Fagen didn’t record another album until 1993, when he reunited with Becker, who produced “Kamakiriad.” The album was promoted by the first Steely Dan tour in nearly 20 years, and while the record failed to sell, the concerts were very popular. In 1995, Steely Dan had another reunion tour, and in early 2000 they released “Two Against Nature,” their first new studio album in two decades, winning a Grammy as Album of the Year. In September 2017, Becker died in Maui, Hawaii at age 67. articles.text: Members of the Hill Branch of UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospital Oakland held a fundraising Valentine’s Dance Party on February 11. Chaired by Sandy Vogl, Carol Leslie, Kris Miller-Fisher, Gretchen Gibson and Laura Giles, the event was an incredible success, raising more than $56,000. Party-goers of all ages filled the University Club level of UC Memorial Stadium in Berkeley to snack on hearty hors d’oeuvres and sip on cocktails. There was a fabulous array of silent auction items to bid on, including Chez Panisse, Cal Athletics, Johnny “Love” Metheny, and numerous wineries including Duckhorn Vineyards and Markham Napa Valley Vineyards. A live band played hits from every era and had the entire crowd dancing until the end of the night. Hill Branch continues to raise money for needs at UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospital Oakland through the Winter Ball. Any variety of dried fruit should work, cherries, cranberries, dates, etc. Rehydrate accordingly to ensure a tender texture in the cake. Apricot and Almond Tea Cake Adapted from Food 52/Sarah Jampel Makes a shallow 10-inch cake INGREDIENTS • 1⁄2 cup unsalted butter, melted and cooled slightly • 1⁄4 cup sour cream • 1 cup granulated sugar, divided 7⁄8 cup for the cake and 1⁄8 cup for the top of the cake • 2 eggs • 11⁄2 cup all-purpose flour • 1⁄2 teaspoon baking soda • 1⁄8 teaspoon salt • 1⁄3 cup dried apricots, diced into 1⁄4-inch pieces • 1 teaspoon fresh lemon zest • 1⁄2 teaspoon almond extract (substitute 1 teaspoon vanilla extract) • 3⁄4 cup sliced almonds INSTRUCTIONS 1. Position an oven rack in the middle position, and preheat oven to 350° F. Generously butter the bottom and sides of a 10-inch pie plate. 2. Rehydrate the diced apricots in a small bowl and cover with warm water. Let sit for 5-10 minutes, then drain the water and spread out on a clean towel to dry the pieces on all sides. You want to get them as dry as possible. This step is optional if your dried fruit is soft and pliable. 3. Combine the flour, baking soda salt in a small bowl. Whisk gently to blend thoroughly. 4. Combine the melted butter, sour cream and 7⁄8’s cup of sugar in a large bowl and mix well to combine. (Can be done either by hand with a sturdy whisk or a hand mixer.) 5. Add the eggs, one at a time, mixing well after each addition. Add the almond extract and lemon zest. 6. Add the flour mixture and mix gently until well incorporated but taking care to avoid over-mixing. Fold in the dried apricots. 7. Pour the batter into the prepared pie plate and smooth to level the surface. Sprinkle the sliced almonds atop in an even layer; then sprinkle on the remaining 1⁄8 cup of granulated sugar in a thin, even layer on top of the sliced almonds. 8. Bake for 30-35 minutes until a toothpick inserted into the center of the cake comes out clean, and the cake and almonds are golden brown. 9. Cool completely before slicing. (The most difficult part of this recipe!) 10. Sit back and smile at what you have created. articles.title: The History of Piedmont

articles.text: Part 11 in a series In the history of Piedmont, two saloons have quenched the thirst of residents and visitors. One saloon was in a respected hotel. The other was fraught with problems. The Piedmont Springs Hotel was built to serve visitors to the Piedmont hills and the mineral springs in Piedmont’s Bushy Dell Creek. Built in 1871 as a first class resort, the hotel had 20 rooms and a main dining room with a crystal chandelier and velvet drapes. The Grand Saloon (for gentlemen only) had a long mahogany bar, billiard table, spittoons and a pot-bellied stove in the corner. The Grand Saloon gained brief notoriety in 1891 when the wives of some of Piedmont’s more prominent businessmen petitioned the county to rescind the hotel’s liquor license. The women objected to their husbands stopping for a drink on their way home. The license was never rescinded, and the Piedmont Springs Hotel continued to serve liquor for another year before it burned to the ground in 1892. A Mon Chateau Piedmont’s other saloon was A Mon Chateau. As far back as the 1870s, today’s Grand Avenue was known as Pleasant Valley Road. It ran through a very pleasant valley – sunny, free of wind, rolling hills, scattered trees – that extended from Lake Merritt into the Piedmont hills. It was the route that many early Oakland residents took from downtown Oakland to picnic in the Piedmont hills. Today, that road is Grand Avenue until it crosses the city line near Rose Avenue. It continues as Pleasant Valley Road in Oakland until it crosses Broadway and becomes 51st Street. In 1892, Axel R. Gruggel built a restaurant at the southwest corner of today’s Grand and Linda Avenues and served refreshments to these travelers into the Piedmont countryside. He called it “A Mon Chateau” (My Castle) and advertised it as a family resort and French restaurant. Taking advantage of the mild weather, he built a beer garden on the Linda Avenue side of the restaurant. During its first years, A Mon Chateau was a quiet, slow-paced retreat, but that changed with the 1906 earthquake. With the influx of San Francisco refugees to the East Bay, the surrounding land began to fill with new houses and residents. From 1903 on, A Mon Chateau had a series of owners with a series of troubles. Gruggel sold the restaurant to George Atcheson in 1903. He ran A Mon Chateau for a few years but encountered problems with his employees stealing liquor. In 1907, three bachelors began operating the restaurant. Thomas P. Fenton, George P. Mahoney and John F. Jennings lived on the second floor of the building and advertised it as “A pleasant place in Pleasant Valley [to eat dinner]. Dinner prepared by Emil Lotz, former chef of Poodle Dog, San Francisco.” Dinners were $1.00. Patrons were advised to take the Oakland Avenue streetcar, get off at Sunnyside Avenue and take a short walk to Pleasant Valley. The bachelor owners also advertised A Mon Chateau as a saloon and sold wine, liquor and cigars besides serving dinners. Soon, neighbors began objecting to what was becoming a boisterous saloon. When the new City of Piedmont (1907) passed its liquor licensing regulations, A Mon Chateau’s application for a liquor license was denied. Nonetheless, the three owners continued to sell liquor at A Mon Chateau without a liquor license. The following year in March 1908, all three were arrested and their liquor confiscated. Three months later in June of 1908, A Mon Chateau opened under new management and continued to advertise itself as a “First Class Restaurant and Family Resort.” New owners Seeger & Thomas continued to operate it as a restaurant, but without a liquor license the number of diners dwindled. In 1911, Rudolph Kohn took over the business. He sought a new way to attract more patrons. He called the former restaurant “The Piedmont Casino” and opened two rooms upstairs for those who enjoyed playing poker and faro. However, gambling was also illegal. The casino was raided in 1912, and nine card-playing patrons were arrested and fined $55 each. The casino closed shortly thereafter. Chateau had become the Grand Avenue Grocery Company, and business thrived. It may not have been a good location for a saloon, but it was an excellent spot for a grocery. Residents in the rapidly growing residential neighborhood could walk to the market at the corner of Grand and Linda Avenues. Proprietors changed, and the grocery business grew. By 1922, the grocery had become the Del Monte Market, run by Jack Ruedy and William VanLoo, who lived upstairs with their wives. The market sold meats, vegetables and delicatessen items. Ruedy and VanLoo added a new storefront, a drug store (Raymond’s Drugs), and built a bakery in the former beer garden to offer freshly baked breads to their customers. In 1930, George W. Leisz and his son Jacob H. Leisz were running the grocery store. The grocery store thrived until 1937 when new supermarkets began pushing out neighborhood grocery stores. Piggly Wiggly opened a supermarket at the other end of the block at Sunnyside and Grand This early photo of A Mon Chateau shows a horse trough in front, Pleasant Valley Road before it was paved, and open rolling hills beyond. “A Mon Chateau” is painted on the gable, and the sign announces “Family Resort.”

From 1903 on, A Mon Chateau had a series of owners with a series of troubles. Gruggel sold the restaurant to George Atcheson in 1903. He ran A Mon Chateau for a few years but encountered problems with his employees stealing liquor. In 1907, three bachelors began operating the restaurant. Thomas P. Fenton, George P. Mahoney and John F. Jennings lived on the second floor of the building and advertised it as “A pleasant place in Pleasant Valley [to eat dinner]. Dinner prepared by Emil Lotz, former chef of Poodle Dog, San Francisco.” Dinners were $1.00. Patrons were advised to take the Oakland Avenue streetcar, get off at Sunnyside Avenue and take a short walk to Pleasant Valley. The bachelor owners also advertised A Mon Chateau as a saloon and sold wine, liquor and cigars besides serving dinners. Soon, neighbors began objecting to what was becoming a boisterous saloon. When the new City of Piedmont (1907) passed its liquor licensing regulations, A Mon Chateau’s application for a liquor license was denied. Nonetheless, the three owners continued to sell liquor at A Mon Chateau without a liquor license. The following year in March 1908, all three were arrested and their liquor confiscated. Three months later in June of 1908, A Mon Chateau opened under new management and continued to advertise itself as a “First Class Restaurant and Family Resort.” New owners Seeger & Thomas continued to operate it as a restaurant, but without a liquor license the number of diners dwindled. In 1911, Rudolph Kohn took over the business. He sought a new way to attract more patrons. He called the former restaurant “The Piedmont Casino” and opened two rooms upstairs for those who enjoyed playing poker and faro. However, gambling was also illegal. The casino was raided in 1912, and nine card-playing patrons were arrested and fined $55 each. The casino closed shortly thereafter. By 1914, the former A Mon Chateau had become the Grand Avenue Grocery Company, and business thrived. It may not have been a good location for a saloon, but it was an excellent spot for a grocery. Residents in the rapidly growing residential neighborhood could walk to the market at the corner of Grand and Linda Avenues. Proprietors changed, and the grocery business grew. By 1922, the grocery had become the Del Monte Market, run by Jack Ruedy and William VanLoo, who lived upstairs with their wives. The market sold meats, vegetables and delicatessen items. Ruedy and VanLoo added a new storefront, a drug store (Raymond’s Drugs), and built a bakery in the former beer garden to offer freshly baked breads to their customers. In 1930, George W. Leisz and his son Jacob H. Leisz were running the grocery store. The grocery store thrived until 1937 when new supermarkets began pushing out neighborhood grocery stores. Piggly Wiggly opened a supermarket at the other end of the block at Sunnyside and Grand Fenton, Maloney and Jennings ran A Mon Chateau in 1907 and 1908. Note the arched opening to the beer garden on the far right. The building was the Grand Avenue Grocery Company in 1915. The grocery enclosed the porch and added large windows. The distinctive gabled roofs of A Mon Chateau are recognizable. (Photo, c. 1915) Avenue, and the Leisz grocery closed in 1935. The old A Mon Chateau building was torn down in 1936 when the Richfield Oil Company built a gas station on the corner lot. In the late 1960s, the business became the Phillips Gas station run by O.N. Gooch and Bernard’s Auto Repair. In the 1970s it became a Chevron Service Station operated by Leo Kraft. When Chevron sold the property in 1987, developer Patrick Ellwood had a two-story building constructed, and Leo Kraft Automotive Service continued in business on the Sunnyside side of the building.
